question: What is soil pH?
answer: Soil pH measures acidity on a 0-14 scale. Below 7 is acidic, above 7 alkaline, 7 is neutral. Your soil at pH {ph} is {ph_direction}. Most crops prefer 5.5-7.0.

question: Why is my soil acidic?
answer: Soil becomes acidic from rainfall leaching calcium, high fertiliser use, and organic matter breakdown. Region {region} rainfall accelerates acidification.

question: How often should I test my soil?

question: What does a pH of 5.1 mean?
answer: pH 5.1 is moderately acidic — below the safe minimum for maize (5.5). Aluminium toxicity becomes a problem below 5.5. Apply lime immediately.

question: What crops grow in acidic soil?
answer: At your pH {ph}: best options are cassava (survives pH 4.5+), sweet potato (5.0+), cowpeas (5.5+), and groundnuts (5.9+).

question: What crops grow in alkaline soil?
answer: Above pH 7.5: barley, wheat, and rape tolerate alkaline conditions best. Avoid groundnuts and potatoes in alkaline soil.

question: What is soil buffering capacity?
answer: Buffering capacity is how strongly soil resists pH change. Clay soils need more lime than sandy soils. Apply lime in split doses — first application, retest after 6 weeks.

question: How does rainfall affect soil pH?
answer: Heavy rainfall leaches calcium and lowers pH over time. Region {region} — test pH every planting season.

question: What is aluminium toxicity?
answer: Below pH 5.5, aluminium dissolves and becomes toxic to roots, stunting growth and blocking phosphorus uptake. Your pH {ph} — apply lime to neutralise if below 5.5.

question: How do I improve my soil overall?
answer: For your {farm_size} ha at pH {ph}: 1) Apply lime if pH below 5.8. 2) Add compost 2 t/ha. 3) Rotate crops. 4) Avoid over-tilling. 5) Keep soil covered.

question: What is organic matter and why does it matter?
answer: Organic matter feeds soil microbes, improves water retention, and releases nutrients slowly. Target 2-4% organic matter. Add 2 t/ha compost per season.

question: How do I make compost?
answer: Layer: crop residues + green waste + manure + soil. Keep moist. Turn every 2 weeks. Ready in 2-3 months. Apply 2 t/ha before planting.

question: What is the difference between clay and sandy soil?
answer: Clay holds water and nutrients well but compacts easily. Sandy soil drains fast with low nutrients. Both need organic matter. Region {region} soils are typically {region_soil_type}.

question: How does soil moisture affect pH readings?
answer: Dry soil can show falsely high pH. Wet soil shows true pH. Your moisture at {moisture}% — test moist (not waterlogged) soil for accurate readings.

question: What is cation exchange capacity?
answer: CEC is how much nutrients soil can hold. Higher clay and organic matter = higher CEC = better nutrient retention. Improve CEC by adding compost each season.

question: How do I prevent soil erosion?
answer: On your {farm_size} ha: plant contour ridges on slopes, use mulch between rows, plant cover crops in off-season, and avoid bare soil during rains.

question: What cover crops can I grow in Zimbabwe?
answer: Best cover crops for Region {region}: lablab (nitrogen fixer), sunhemp (fast biomass), velvet bean. Slash and incorporate 2-3 weeks before planting.

question: How do I reduce soil compaction?
answer: Avoid field operations when soil is wet. Use minimum tillage. Add organic matter. Subsoil once every 3 years if compaction is severe.

question: Can I grow crops in clay soil?
answer: Yes. Clay soil is nutrient-rich. Improve drainage by adding compost, creating ridges or raised beds, and planting on slight slopes.

question: Can I grow crops in sandy soil?
answer: Yes. Sandy soil drains fast — add compost to improve water retention. Irrigate more frequently. Mulch between rows. Groundnuts and cassava do well in sandy soils.

question: What nutrients does my soil need?
answer: Primary: Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), Potassium (K). Secondary: Calcium, Magnesium, Sulphur. Your pH {ph} affects nutrient availability significantly.

question: What is nitrogen and why do crops need it?
answer: Nitrogen drives leaf growth and chlorophyll. Deficiency = yellow leaves, stunted growth. Apply AN 34.5% at vegetative stage. Legumes fix their own nitrogen from air.

question: What is phosphorus and why do crops need it?
answer: Phosphorus drives root development and flowering. Apply at planting as Compound D or SSP. At pH {ph}, phosphorus availability varies.

question: What is potassium and why do crops need it?
answer: Potassium regulates water use and disease resistance. Deficiency = brown leaf edges, weak stems. Apply MOP or use compound fertilisers containing K.

question: What is the NPK ratio in Compound D?
answer: Compound D: 7% N, 14% P, 7% K plus sulphur. Best applied at planting at 200 kg/ha. For your {farm_size} ha: {compound_d_total} kg total.

question: What fertiliser should I apply first?
answer: At planting: Compound D (7:14:7). At vegetative stage (V6): AN 34.5% as topdress. Standard two-application programme for Region {region}.

question: How do I know if my soil needs fertiliser?
answer: Signs of deficiency: yellow leaves (nitrogen), purple tinge (phosphorus), brown edges (potassium). Your soil at pH {ph} — {ph_fert_advice}.

question: What is micronutrient deficiency?
answer: Zinc deficiency is common in Zimbabwe — causes striped leaves in maize. Apply zinc sulphate at 10 kg/ha or use Compound C which contains zinc.

question: How does pH affect fertiliser effectiveness?
answer: At pH {ph}: nutrients may be locked out — lime before fertilising. Nutrients are unavailable in acidic soil and you waste money on fertiliser the plant cannot absorb.

question: What is waterlogging?
answer: Waterlogged soil has no oxygen — roots suffocate. Your moisture at {moisture}% — plant on ridges or raised beds if waterlogging is common on your land.

question: What is a soil test?
answer: Laboratory analysis of soil nutrient levels, pH, and organic matter. Costs $10-25 per sample. Recommended every 3 years. Available through AGRITEX and private labs in Harare and Bulawayo.

question: What is liming frequency?
answer: In Region {region}: lime every 2-3 years on acidic soils. Annual small applications are more effective than large occasional doses. Your current pH {ph} determines urgency.

question: What is gypsum used for?
answer: Gypsum (calcium sulphate) improves subsoil structure and provides calcium and sulphur without raising pH. Used on compacted or sodic soils. Apply 500 kg/ha incorporated.

question: What is compost vs manure?
answer: Compost: decomposed plant/food waste — balanced nutrients, improves structure. Manure: animal waste — higher nitrogen but pathogens if fresh. Both improve soil. Apply 2-5 t/ha annually.

question: What is green manure?
answer: Incorporating a growing crop (lablab, sunhemp) into the soil while still green — adds organic matter and nutrients. Cut at flowering stage, incorporate, wait 2-3 weeks before planting.

question: What is soil respiration?
answer: Biological activity in soil — decomposition of organic matter by microbes. Healthy soil has high respiration. Improve by: adding organic matter, correct pH, adequate moisture, avoiding compaction.

question: What is my soil moisture?

question: Is my soil too dry?
answer: At {moisture}% moisture — below 30% is critical. Irrigate immediately if available. Mulch to conserve remaining moisture.

question: Is my soil too wet?
answer: At {moisture}% moisture — above 80% risks root oxygen deprivation. Improve drainage and avoid field operations.

question: When should I irrigate?
answer: Irrigate when moisture drops below 40-45%. Your current reading is {moisture}% — act accordingly. Critical periods for {crop}: germination and flowering.

question: How much water does maize need?
answer: Maize needs 500-800mm total. Critical: germination (week 1-2), tasselling (week 8-10), grain fill (week 10-14). Below 40% at these stages causes permanent yield loss.

question: How much water does sugar beans need?
answer: Sugar beans need 350-500mm. Drought-tolerant after establishment. Avoid waterlogging at any stage. Your {moisture}% is within acceptable range.

question: How much water does sorghum need?
answer: Sorghum needs only 300-400mm — most drought-tolerant cereal. Very suitable for Region {region} conditions.

question: What is drip irrigation?
answer: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to roots via pipes and emitters. Uses 40-60% less water than flood irrigation. Excellent for high-value vegetables.

question: What is furrow irrigation?
answer: Water flows along furrows between crop rows. Cheap and common in Zimbabwe. Risk of waterlogging. Best for maize and sugar cane.

question: How do I conserve soil moisture?
answer: Mulch between rows — reduces evaporation by 30-50%. Tie ridges to catch runoff. Plant early to use seasonal rains. Minimum tillage reduces moisture loss.

question: What is moisture stress?
answer: Moisture stress is water deficit during critical growth stages. At {moisture}% — permanent damage occurs below 25% at tasselling in maize.

question: How does temperature affect water needs?
answer: At {temp}C, evapotranspiration increases. Higher temperature = more water loss. Irrigate in early morning or evening to reduce evaporation.

question: What is field capacity?
answer: Field capacity is maximum water soil holds after drainage — typically 40-70% volumetric. Your {moisture}% reading shows current status.

question: What is the permanent wilting point?
answer: Below 15-20% moisture, plants cannot extract water and wilt permanently. Your {moisture}% — act before moisture drops below 30%.

question: How do I measure soil moisture without a sensor?
answer: Squeeze test: grab soil at 10cm depth. Ball forms and stays = adequate. Crumbles = too dry. Water squeezes out = too wet.

question: What is water harvesting?
answer: Collect and store rainwater: tie ridges, contour bunds, small dams, zai pits. Critical in Region {region} where rainfall is variable.

question: What are zai pits?
answer: Small planting pits (30x30x15cm) that concentrate water and nutrients at each plant. Used in semi-arid areas. Effective in Regions IV and V.

question: What is deficit irrigation?
answer: Applying less than full crop water requirement — accepts some yield reduction to save water. 80% of full requirement causes less than 10% yield loss in most crops.

question: How does rainfall vary across Zimbabwe?
answer: Region I: 1000mm+. Region II: 750-1000mm. Region III: 650-800mm. Region IV: 450-650mm. Region V: under 450mm. You are in Region {region}.

question: When does the rainy season start?
answer: In Region {region}: rains typically start in October-November. Plant within 2 weeks of first reliable rains. Do not plant into dry soil expecting rain.

question: How do I manage runoff?
answer: Prevent runoff with: tied ridges across slope, contour ploughing, grass strips every 10-15m, cover crops. Runoff takes topsoil.

question: What is mulching?
answer: Mulching covers soil with organic material — grass, straw, crop residues. Reduces evaporation, controls weeds, moderates soil temperature, adds organic matter.

question: What is tie ridging?
answer: Earthen barriers built across furrows to trap rainwater in-field. Creates small reservoirs. Very effective in Regions III-V where rain is erratic.

question: What is minimum tillage?
answer: Reducing or eliminating ploughing — use ripping instead of full inversion. Preserves soil structure, reduces moisture loss, saves fuel. Best practice for communal areas.

question: What is conservation agriculture?
answer: Three principles: minimum soil disturbance, permanent soil cover, crop rotation. Builds soil health over seasons. Endorsed by AGRITEX for smallholder farmers.

question: How do I judge rain intensity?
answer: Light rain under 5mm/hr soaks in. Moderate 5-15mm/hr causes some runoff. Heavy above 15mm/hr causes significant runoff and erosion risk.

question: What is soil moisture monitoring?
answer: Track moisture over time to understand water-holding capacity and decide irrigation timing. Your sensor shows {moisture}% — compare week to week.

question: How does soil type affect water retention?
answer: Clay holds more water — good in drought. Sandy drains fast — needs more frequent irrigation. Add compost to improve water holding regardless of soil type.

question: Can I grow crops in the dry season?
answer: Yes — with irrigation. Best dry-season crops for Region {region}: cabbages, rape, onions, garlic, tomatoes, sugar beans. Your irrigation status: {irrigation_status}.

question: How does wind affect soil moisture?
answer: Wind increases evapotranspiration — drying soil faster. Plant windbreaks on windward side. Water more frequently on windy days.

question: What is evapotranspiration?
answer: Combined water loss from soil evaporation and plant transpiration. At {temp}C in Region {region}: significant water demand. Guides irrigation scheduling.

question: Can I use borehole water for irrigation?
answer: Yes — check borehole water pH and salt content first. Hard water may raise soil pH over time. Flush soil periodically with rainfall.

question: What is micro-irrigation?
answer: Small-scale drip or sprinkler systems for small plots — as small as 0.1 ha. Low-cost kits available from AGRITEX and NGOs.

question: What is bucket drip irrigation?
answer: Elevated bucket with drip tape — no pump needed. Gravity-fed. Cost $20-50 for 0.05 ha plot. Very effective for high-value vegetables.

question: How do I prevent drought damage?
answer: Plant drought-tolerant varieties, mulch heavily, irrigate before stress not after, plant at correct time, use shorter-season varieties in dry years.

question: What are drought-tolerant crops?
answer: Most drought-tolerant for Region {region}: sorghum (350mm), pearl millet (250mm), sesame (300mm), cowpeas (300mm), groundnuts (400mm). Maize needs 500mm+.

question: How does plant spacing affect water use?
answer: Wider spacing reduces competition for water. In dry years reduce plant population by 10-15%. Maize: 75x25cm standard, 90x30cm in dry conditions.

question: What is the water table?
answer: Depth to underground water. High water table near surface = waterlogging risk. Low water table = borehole needed. Ask local farmers about typical depth.

question: How do I reduce evaporation from soil?
answer: Mulch (most effective), shade cloth on small plots, furrow irrigation keeps surface drier than sprinkler, minimum tillage reduces evaporation.

question: What is grey water recycling?
answer: Using household wash water on gardens. Safe for vegetables if biodegradable soap used. Apply at root zone, not on leaves of leafy vegetables.

question: What is a dambo?
answer: Seasonal wetland — low-lying flat area that stays moist through dry season. Often used for dry-season vegetable gardens. Rich soils but may flood in wet season.

question: What is runoff coefficient?
answer: Proportion of rainfall that runs off vs soaks in. Bare soil: 60-80% runoff. Mulched soil: 10-20% runoff. Crop residues greatly improve infiltration.

question: What is soil texture vs soil structure?
answer: Texture = sand/silt/clay ratio (fixed). Structure = how particles are arranged (can be improved). Improve structure with compost and minimum tillage.

question: How do I deal with waterlogged fields?
answer: Install drainage channels at field edges. Plant on raised ridges. Avoid field operations when wet. Choose flood-tolerant crops if flooding is regular.

question: What is a rain gauge?
answer: A rain gauge measures rainfall in mm. Place at field edge away from trees. Record after every rain. Your Region {region} seasonal target: 650-1000mm depending on exact zone.

question: What is morning dew?
answer: Dew provides 0.1-0.3mm equivalent moisture per night. Not enough to replace rainfall but helps maintain surface moisture in dry periods.

question: What is crop water productivity?
answer: Yield per unit of water used. Sorghum: 0.8-1.2 kg/mm. Maize: 0.5-0.9 kg/mm. Choose high water-productivity crops in water-limited Region {region} conditions.

question: How much water does a borehole provide?
answer: Typical communal borehole: 1-3 cubic metres per hour. For 1 ha of maize needing 600mm/season: approximately 600 cubic metres total — 200-600 hours pumping per hectare.

question: What is a contour ridge?
answer: An earthen bank built along a contour line to slow runoff and increase infiltration. Space every 10-20m on sloped land. Combined with tie ridges: excellent water harvesting.

question: What is soil water depletion?
answer: As plants grow they extract water from soil — depleting stored reserves. Monitor with sensor. Replenish by rain or irrigation before reaching wilting point of 20-25%.

question: When should I plant maize?
answer: In Region {region}, plant maize at first reliable rains in October-December. Plant into moist soil. Your current moisture {moisture}% is adequate for planting.

question: What maize variety should I plant?
answer: For {budget} budget in Region {region}: ZM521 (low budget, OPV), SC403 (medium, hybrid), SC627 (high, hybrid). Expected yield at {budget} input in Region {region}: 2.5-6 t/ha.

question: What is the best plant spacing for maize?
answer: Standard: 75cm between rows x 25cm between plants = 53,000 plants/ha. Plant 2 seeds per station, thin to 1 at V3.

question: How deep should I plant maize?
answer: 3-5cm deep in moist soil. Deeper in dry conditions (up to 7cm) to reach moisture. Shallower in cool, wet conditions to speed germination.

question: What fertiliser does maize need?
answer: Planting: Compound D 7:14:7 at 200 kg/ha. Topdress at V6: AN 34.5% at 200 kg/ha. For your {farm_size} ha: {compound_d_total} kg Compound D + {an_total} kg AN.

question: When do I apply topdress fertiliser?
answer: Apply AN 34.5% at V6 stage — approximately 35 days after emergence. Your crop at day {days_planted} — check Calendar tab for exact timing.

question: How do I know if my crop needs nitrogen?
answer: Signs: yellowing starting from leaf tip on lower leaves, V-shaped yellow pattern on leaf. Apply AN 34.5% immediately on sight of these signs.

question: What is the V6 stage?
answer: V6 = 6 visible leaf collars on the maize plant. Count from ground up. Typically at 30-40 days after planting. Critical fertiliser application timing.

question: What is tasselling?
answer: When the male flower emerges from the top of the plant — signals reproductive stage. Occurs 55-70 days after planting. Critical water stage — never stress at tasselling.

question: What is the silking stage?
answer: When silk strands emerge from the ear. Pollen falls from tassel onto silk — fertilisation. Drought during silking causes barren cobs with missing kernels.

question: What causes poor germination?
answer: Causes: seed too deep or shallow, soil too dry or wet, old seed, soil below 15C, seed rot from fungal disease, birds or rodents. Your soil at {temp}C — {germ_temp_status}.

question: What is gap filling?
answer: Replanting empty stands within 7-10 days of planting — before established plants shade out gaps. Use same variety. Mark gaps with sticks to find them.

question: When should I weed?
answer: First weeding: 2-3 weeks after emergence. Critical: keep weed-free for first 6 weeks. Weeds after 6 weeks cause less than 10% yield loss. Second weeding at V6.

question: How do I control weeds cheaply?
answer: Hand weeding at V3. Cultivate between rows at V6. Mulch between rows. Correct plant spacing shades out weeds.

question: What herbicide can I use on maize?
answer: Pre-emergence: Atrazine 2-3 L/ha within 3 days of planting on moist soil. Post-emergence: Nicosulfuron at V3-V5 for grass weeds. Do not spray in hot conditions above 30C.

question: What is intercropping?
answer: Growing two crops together in the same field. Common: maize + sugar beans, maize + cowpeas. Benefits: better land use, nitrogen fixation, risk spreading.

question: Should I intercrop maize and sugar beans?
answer: Yes — very suitable for Region {region} at {budget} budget. Plant sugar beans in alternate rows 2-3 weeks after maize. Beans fix nitrogen. Combined yield often exceeds monocrop returns.

question: What is crop rotation?
answer: Changing crop family each season. Maize → legume (sugar beans/groundnuts) → brassica (rape/cabbage). Minimum 2-year rotation. Breaks pest cycles and restores soil nitrogen.

question: Why should I rotate crops?
answer: Rotation breaks Fall Armyworm and stalk borer cycles. Legumes fix nitrogen for next crop. Reduces disease build-up. Improves soil organic matter.

question: What crop should I grow after maize?
answer: After maize: grow sugar beans or groundnuts. They fix 50-150 kg N/ha — saving fertiliser for next maize season. Your pH {ph} suits legume rotation.

question: What is a cover crop?
answer: Fast-growing crop planted after harvest to protect soil and add organic matter. Lablab, sunnhemp, and velvet bean are best for Zimbabwe. Slash and incorporate 4 weeks before planting.

question: What is thinning?
answer: Removing excess plants to leave optimal plant population. For maize: thin to 1 plant per station at V2-V3 (10-14 days after emergence). Do not thin later.

question: What is hilling up?
answer: Pushing soil up around maize stalks at V6-V8. Improves anchorage, covers surface roots, and buries early stalk borers. Do during second cultivation.

question: What is lodging?
answer: Maize stalks falling over — from weak roots, stalk borer, wind, or waterlogging. Prevent by: hilling up, not over-applying nitrogen, controlling stalk borer early.

question: What is seed priming?
answer: Soaking seeds in water for 8-12 hours before planting — improves germination speed and uniformity. Use clean water. Spread seeds to dry slightly before planting.

question: What is seed treatment?
answer: Coating seeds with fungicide or insecticide before planting. Protects against soil-borne disease and early insect attack. Many commercial seeds are pre-treated (pink or red colour).

question: What is transplanting?
answer: Moving seedlings from nursery to field. Used for tomatoes, cabbages, onions. Transplant in late afternoon or cloudy days. Water immediately after transplanting.

question: How do I make a seedling nursery?
answer: Prepare raised beds 1m wide. Fill with compost-rich soil. Sow seeds thinly. Water twice daily. Shade for first week. Harden off by reducing watering 1 week before transplanting.

question: What is crop staging?
answer: Identifying growth stage by visible plant features — V stages (vegetative) and R stages (reproductive) in maize. Used to time fertiliser, pesticide, and irrigation correctly.

question: What are the V stages of maize?
answer: V1 = first leaf collar. V6 = 6 collars. VT = tassel visible. Each stage takes 5-7 days. Your crop at day {days_planted} is approximately at the right stage.

question: What is topdressing?
answer: Applying nitrogen fertiliser (AN 34.5% or CAN) to growing crops at V6. Broadcast between rows and water in or apply before rain.

question: What is basal application?
answer: Applying fertiliser at planting in furrow or planting hole. Use Compound D. Place 5cm away from seed to avoid burning.

question: What is seed viability?
answer: Percentage of seeds that will germinate. Maize: 85%+ is good. Test before planting: 10 seeds on wet cloth, count after 5-7 days. Replace if below 70%.

question: What is expected yield for maize?
answer: Maize yield in Region {region} at {budget} input: 2.5-6 t/ha. For your {farm_size} ha: approximately {maize_total_yield} kg. At $0.28/kg: ${maize_revenue} gross revenue.

question: What is expected yield for sugar beans?
answer: Sugar beans at {budget} input: 0.6-1.5 t/ha. For your {farm_size} ha: 1,440-3,600 kg. At $0.65/kg: $936-$2,340 gross.

question: What is expected yield for sorghum?
answer: Sorghum at {budget} input: 1.0-4.0 t/ha. Drought year in Region {region}: expect lower end. For {farm_size} ha: 2,400-9,600 kg total.

question: How do I improve my yield?
answer: Top 5 yield improvements: 1) Fix pH {ph} to 6.0+ with lime. 2) Use certified seed. 3) Apply Compound D at planting. 4) Topdress AN at V6. 5) Control Fall Armyworm in first 4 weeks.

question: What is the yield gap?
answer: Difference between potential yield and actual farmer yield. For Region {region} maize: potential 8-10 t/ha, typical smallholder 1-3 t/ha. Close the gap: correct pH, certified seed, timely operations.

question: What is a farming calendar?
answer: Month-by-month schedule of field operations. Follow the Calendar tab for your {crop} crop with daily task details.

question: What is land preparation?
answer: Ploughing, discing, and ridging before planting. Complete at least 2 weeks before planting. Destroys weeds, improves soil structure, conserves moisture.

question: When should I plough?
answer: In Region {region}: plough at end of dry season or early wet season. Deep plough (25cm) once every 3 years. Minimum till in between.

question: What is the best plant spacing for groundnuts?
answer: Groundnuts: 45cm between rows x 15cm between plants. Plant single seeds 3-5cm deep. Do not plant pods — shell first. Firm soil around seed.

question: What is the best plant spacing for sugar beans?
answer: Sugar beans: 45-60cm between rows x 10cm between plants. 2 seeds per station, thin to 1 at emergence. Do not intercrop with maize unless experienced.

question: What is the best plant spacing for sorghum?
answer: Sorghum: 75cm between rows x 20cm between plants. Thin to 2-3 plants per station. Can handle higher density than maize — more flexible with spacing.

question: What is thinning and when do I do it?
answer: Removing excess plants at 10-14 days after emergence when plants are 10-15cm tall. For maize: 1 plant per station. Sugar beans: 1-2 plants. Groundnuts: 2 plants per station.

question: How do I prevent crop failure?
answer: Plant at correct time (optimal window for Region {region}). Use good seed. Apply correct fertiliser. Scout for pests weekly. Have contingency plan — savings or crop insurance.

question: What is ratoon cropping?
answer: Allowing a crop to regrow from the stump after harvest. Common in sorghum. Not recommended for maize. Ratoons yield poorly and harbour pests.

question: What is a catch crop?
answer: Short-season crop planted after early harvest to use remaining season. Cowpeas and sugar beans as catch crops add value to the tail of the season.

question: What is harvest index?
answer: Ratio of grain yield to total plant biomass. Maize: 0.45-0.55. Modern hybrids have higher harvest index than OPV varieties — more grain per unit of plant growth.

question: What pests should I watch for?
answer: For {crop} in Region {region}: top threats are Fall Armyworm (critical), Maize Stalk Borer (high), and Aphids (medium). Scout weekly — check 20 plants per hectare.

question: How do I identify Fall Armyworm?
answer: Look for: window-pane feeding on young leaves, sawdust-like frass in the whorl, ragged holes in older leaves, and caterpillars in the whorl at night with Y-mark on head.

question: How do I treat Fall Armyworm organically?
answer: Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) DiPel: 1 kg/ha in 200L water. Apply into whorl before caterpillars enter. Early morning application. Repeat after 5 days. Cost for {farm_size} ha: approximately ${faw_organic_cost}.

question: How do I treat Fall Armyworm chemically?
answer: Emamectin benzoate (Proclaim) 0.2 kg/ha or Chlorpyrifos (Dursban) 1.5 L/ha. Apply into whorl. Use at V3-V6 before caterpillars enter stalk. Wear full PPE.

question: What is the economic threshold for Fall Armyworm?
answer: Treat when more than 30% of plants show active infestation with live caterpillars. Spot-treat high-infestation patches first rather than blanket application.

question: How do I scout for pests?
answer: Walk W or X pattern across field. Check 20 plants per hectare at 4-5 locations. Look at both leaf surfaces, in whorl, and at base of stalk. Record % plants infested.

question: What is maize stalk borer?
answer: Busseola fusca — caterpillar that bores into maize stalk. Signs: dead heart in young plants, row of holes across leaves, sawdust frass. Treat at first sign — cannot control once inside stalk.

question: How do I control maize stalk borer?
answer: Apply Carbofuran granules into whorl at V3-V5: 2 granules per plant. Or Chlorpyrifos spray into whorl. Sand + Carbofuran mix: 1 kg granules in 5 kg fine sand.

question: What causes yellow leaves?
answer: Yellow leaves indicate: nitrogen deficiency (V-pattern from tip), iron deficiency (interveinal yellowing), waterlogging (all lower leaves), or Maize Streak Virus (yellow streaks).

question: What is Maize Streak Virus?
answer: Spread by leafhopper insects. Symptoms: yellow streaks on leaves, stunted plants. No cure — remove infected plants. Prevent: plant early, use tolerant varieties (ZM521 is tolerant).

question: What is grey leaf spot?
answer: Fungal disease — long rectangular grey-tan lesions on lower leaves moving upward. Worse in humid conditions. Apply Propiconazole (Tilt) at first signs. Rotate crops.

question: What is northern corn leaf blight?
answer: Fungal disease — cigar-shaped grey-green lesions on lower leaves. Worse in cool, wet conditions. Apply Propiconazole or Azoxystrobin at first sign. Ensure crop rotation.

question: What is Phytophthora root rot?
answer: Fungal disease in waterlogged soils — plants collapse and die. No effective chemical control. Prevent: improve drainage, plant on ridges, avoid waterlogged areas.

question: What are aphids?
answer: Small soft-bodied insects, green or black, clustered on leaves and stems. Suck plant sap. Spray with Dimethoate or Pirimicarb. Organic: soap spray (50g/L water).

question: What are thrips?
answer: Tiny insects that rasp leaf surfaces causing silver streaks and distorted growth. Worse in dry conditions. Spray Abamectin or Spinosad. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides.

question: What is bean rust?
answer: Fungal disease on sugar beans and cowpeas — orange-brown pustules on leaf undersides. Apply Mancozeb or Chlorothalonil at first sign. Plant resistant varieties.

question: What is powdery mildew?
answer: White powdery coating on leaves — common on cucurbits and legumes. Apply sulphur dust or Triadimefon. Improve air circulation. Water at base not on leaves.

question: What is damping off?
answer: Seedling disease — stems rot at soil level. Caused by Pythium and Fusarium in wet, cold conditions. Treat seed with Metalaxyl. Improve drainage. Do not overwater seedlings.

question: What are nematodes?
answer: Microscopic worms in soil — root knot nematodes cause galls on roots, stunted plants. Common in sandy soils. Rotate with non-host crops to break cycle.

question: What are cutworms?
answer: Fat grey/brown caterpillars that cut seedlings at soil level at night. Apply Chlorpyrifos to soil before planting or place poisoned bran baits around seedlings.

question: What are armyworms?
answer: Spodoptera spp. — mass migrations in swarms, attack grass and small grains. Apply Chlorpyrifos or Lambda-cyhalothrin (Karate) immediately on sight.

question: What are termites?
answer: Termites attack dead plant material and sometimes live roots in dry conditions. Treat soil with Chlorpyrifos before planting. Keep soil moist — termites prefer dry conditions.

question: How do I prevent diseases?
answer: Prevention package: 1) Certified disease-resistant seed. 2) Correct plant spacing for air circulation. 3) Rotate crops. 4) Remove infected plants. 5) Correct pH {ph}.

question: What is integrated pest management?
answer: IPM uses multiple methods in order: prevention, then cultural control (spacing, rotation), then biological control (Bt), then chemical as last resort. More sustainable and cheaper.

question: What spray equipment do I need?
answer: For {farm_size} ha: a 15-20L knapsack sprayer ($25-40) handles up to 2 ha per day. Always calibrate sprayer before use — incorrect calibration wastes product.

question: How do I calibrate a knapsack sprayer?
answer: Fill with water, spray 1 minute, measure output. Standard: 15L per 15 minutes = 1L/minute. Adjust to achieve 200L water per hectare coverage.

question: What PPE do I need for spraying?
answer: Minimum: rubber gloves, wellington boots, long-sleeved clothes, hat. For concentrated chemicals: goggles, face shield, respirator. Wash clothes after spraying.

question: When is the best time to spray?
answer: Early morning (6-9am) or late afternoon (4-6pm). Avoid midday heat — reduces effectiveness. Avoid windy conditions. Avoid before rain — washes off product.

question: How do I store chemicals safely?
answer: Original container, locked store away from food and children. Cool, dry, ventilated location. Never near water sources. Triple-rinse and puncture empty containers.

question: What is pesticide resistance?
answer: Pests become resistant when same chemical is used repeatedly. Rotate chemical groups — alternate Organophosphates, Pyrethroids, and Biologicals. Resistance is permanent.

question: What are biological controls?
answer: Using natural enemies: Bt for caterpillars, Beauveria bassiana for aphids and thrips, predatory wasps for stem borers, ladybirds for aphids. Safe and sustainable.

question: What is a pheromone trap?
answer: Sex-attractant lures to catch adult moths (Fall Armyworm, Stalk Borer). Used for monitoring not control. 4-6 traps per ha. Check weekly — tells you when pest populations are rising.

question: What is the pre-harvest interval?
answer: Days between last chemical application and harvest. Always check product label. Violation risks consumer health. Observe strictly for food safety.

question: How do I dispose of pesticide containers?
answer: Triple rinse (add water, shake, empty into sprayer). Puncture bottom. Bury in designated pit away from water sources. Never burn — toxic fumes.

question: What is the difference between contact and systemic pesticides?
answer: Contact: kills pests it touches directly. Systemic: absorbed by plant, kills sucking insects feeding on sap. Use systemic for aphids. Use contact for caterpillars.

question: What is Atrazine?
answer: Pre-emergence herbicide for maize — controls broadleaf weeds before they emerge. Apply within 3 days of planting on moist soil.

question: What is a fungicide?
answer: Chemical that controls fungal diseases. Contact fungicides (Mancozeb) protect leaf surface. Systemic (Propiconazole) move inside plant. Alternate groups to prevent resistance.

question: What is an insecticide?
answer: Chemical that kills insects. Carbamates (Carbofuran), Organophosphates (Dimethoate), Pyrethroids (Lambda-cyhalothrin), Biologicals (Bt). Choose based on pest type.

question: What is a herbicide?
answer: Chemical that kills plants (weeds). Selective herbicides kill specific weeds without harming the crop. Non-selective (Glyphosate) kills all plants — use only before crop emergence.

question: What is Glyphosate?
answer: Non-selective systemic herbicide — kills all green plants. Use for land clearing before planting, or between rows with a wiper applicator. Never spray on crop leaves.

question: Are there organic pest control options?
answer: Yes. Neem extract 50mL/L water. Wood ash dusted on leaves. Soap solution 50g soap/L water kills soft-bodied insects. Bt for caterpillars. All safe and biodegradable.

question: What is neem extract?
answer: Pressed from neem seeds — contains azadirachtin that disrupts insect growth. Apply 50mL/L water. Effective against aphids, thrips, whitefly. Safe and locally available.

question: What is grey mould (botrytis)?
answer: Fungal disease causing grey fuzzy mould on flowers, leaves, and fruit. Common in cool, humid conditions. Remove infected parts. Improve air circulation. Apply Iprodione if severe.

question: What is fusarium wilt?
answer: Soil-borne fungal disease causing wilting and yellowing of one side of plant. Vascular tissue shows brown discolouration. No chemical cure. Rotate crops. Use resistant varieties.

question: What is anthracnose?
answer: Fungal disease causing dark sunken lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit. Common in beans, sorghum, and tomatoes. Apply Mancozeb or Chlorothalonil. Remove and destroy infected material.

question: What is downy mildew?
answer: Fungal disease causing yellow patches on upper leaf surface with grey fuzzy growth below. Common in maize and vegetables in wet conditions. Apply Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (Ridomil Gold).

question: What is bacterial blight?
answer: Water-soaked lesions that turn brown and dry out — common in beans and maize. Spread by rain splash. Copper fungicides provide some control. Use clean certified seed.

question: What is brown streak virus?
answer: Cassava disease causing yellow streaks and necrosis in tubers — major threat to food security. Spread by whitefly. Plant certified clean planting material. Remove and burn infected plants.

question: What is maize lethal necrosis?
answer: Combination of two viruses causing rapid plant death. Not yet confirmed widespread in Zimbabwe. Monitor for: yellowing, drying, plant death from tips downward before reproductive stage.

question: What is a thrips infestation?
answer: Silvery streaks or bronzing on leaves, flower drop, distorted growth. Check with magnifying glass — tiny insects in flower buds. Spray Spinosad (Tracer) or Abamectin (Dynamec).

question: When should I harvest maize?
answer: Harvest when: grain moisture below 25%, black layer visible at grain base, kernels hard and dented, husk is dry and papery. For ZM521 in Region {region}: approximately 120 days from planting.

question: How do I tell if maize is ready to harvest?
answer: Press thumbnail into kernel — if no dent forms, ready. Tear back husk — kernels should be dry and hard. Check black layer at kernel base. Silk should be completely dry.

question: What is the black layer test?
answer: The black layer forms at the grain base when grain reaches physiological maturity. Snap off a few grains — a black layer means maximum yield is achieved and grain is ready.

question: What grain moisture is safe for storage?
answer: Below 12.5% for safe long-term storage. 13-14% for short-term (1-3 months). Above 14% promotes mould growth and aflatoxin. Grain should bite cleanly without sticking.

question: How do I dry maize after harvest?
answer: Spread on clean tarpaulin in direct sun. Turn 2-3 times daily. Takes 7-14 days. Shell only after drying to target moisture. Do not store undried maize.

question: How do I shell maize?
answer: By hand rubbing for small quantities. Motorised sheller: $0.50-1.00/bag service charge. Shell only when dry — wet shelling damages kernels and increases disease entry.

question: What are hermetic bags?
answer: Airtight grain storage bags that kill grain-boring insects by oxygen depletion. Brands: PICS triple bag, GrainSafe, ZeroFly. Cost $2-4 per 50kg bag. Reusable 3-5 seasons. Endorsed by FAO.

question: How do I use hermetic bags?
answer: Fill completely — no air gaps. Seal tightly — twist, fold, and tie inner bag, then outer bag. Store off ground on wooden pallet. Keep in cool, dry, ventilated store.

question: What is aflatoxin?
answer: Toxic compound produced by Aspergillus mould in poorly stored grain. Causes liver cancer with long-term exposure. Invisible. Prevent: dry below 12.5% moisture, use hermetic bags.

question: How do I prevent aflatoxin?
answer: 1) Harvest at right time. 2) Dry rapidly to below 12.5% moisture. 3) Store in hermetic bags. 4) Sort and remove broken/mouldy grains. 5) Store in cool, dry conditions.

question: What is grain weevil?
answer: Sitophilus zeamais — most common grain storage pest in Zimbabwe. Bores into grain, lays eggs inside. Signs: fine dust, holed kernels. Prevent with hermetic bags or Actellic Super dust.

question: How do I treat grain for storage?
answer: Option 1: Hermetic bags (no chemical — preferred). Option 2: Actellic Super dust — 50g per 90kg bag. Mix thoroughly before storage. Follow label instructions.

question: How long can I store maize?
answer: Hermetic bags: 12+ months at below 12.5% moisture. Open sacks: 3-6 months if treated. Traditional granaries: 3-4 months. Hermetic storage is the difference between profit and loss.

question: How do I build a grain store?
answer: Raised floor (60cm minimum) on brick pillars. Ventilated walls. Rat-proof by fitting metal flashing around pillars. Roof overhang to keep walls dry. Clean before new stock.

question: What is post-harvest loss?
answer: Grain lost between harvest and consumption through pests, mould, spillage. Average Zimbabwe post-harvest loss: 15-30% without hermetic storage. Hermetic bags reduce this to under 2%.

question: How do I market my maize?
answer: Options: Grain Marketing Board (GMB) at fixed price, private buyers, local market. Check GMB producer price before harvest — compare to private buyers.

question: Should I sell immediately after harvest or store?
answer: Prices typically rise 20-40% from March to August. Storing in hermetic bags until June-August can significantly improve returns. Risk: price may not rise if bumper national harvest.

question: What is value addition?
answer: Processing grain to increase value: milling maize into mealie meal, processing groundnuts into peanut butter, drying vegetables. Adds 30-100% to raw commodity value.

question: What is contract farming?
answer: Signing an agreement with a buyer before planting — guaranteed price and sometimes input supply. Companies like SeedCo, Innscor offer contract schemes. Reduces price risk.

question: How do I prevent rodents in my grain store?
answer: Metal flashing on storage pillars, snap traps inside store, block all entry holes larger than 1cm, keep area around store clear of debris. Never use poison near stored food grain.

question: What causes grain to clump together?
answer: High moisture — grain should be below 12.5% before storage. Clumping means mould is starting. Spread grain immediately in sun. Remove and discard visibly mouldy grain.

question: What is grain moisture content?
answer: Percentage of water in grain by weight. Safe storage: 12.5% or below. Measure with a moisture meter ($20-50). Field test: press grain with teeth — should crack cleanly.

question: How do I harvest sugar beans?
answer: Harvest when 80% of pods are dry and yellow-brown. Pull plants by hand or cut at base. Dry on tarpaulin for 7-10 days. Thresh by beating against drum. Winnow to remove debris.

question: How do I store sugar beans?
answer: Dry to 12% moisture. Store in hermetic bags — beans are very susceptible to bean weevil. Weevil can destroy 100% of beans in 3 months in open storage.

question: How do I harvest groundnuts?
answer: Harvest when most leaves have yellowed and pods are mature (brown veining inside pod). Lift with hoe — shake off soil. Dry standing for 1-2 weeks. Strip pods, dry further.

question: What is aflatoxin in groundnuts?
answer: Groundnuts are especially susceptible to aflatoxin if dried slowly or stored damp. Harvest before rains, dry rapidly, remove damaged pods. Major export rejection cause.

question: How do I harvest sorghum?
answer: Harvest when grain is hard and cannot be crushed easily. Cut heads with panga. Dry on tarpaulin. Thresh by beating heads against drum. Clean and dry to 12% before storage.

question: What is proper maize shelling?
answer: Shell only dry maize (below 14% moisture). Motorised sheller gives cleaner grain. Hand-shelling: two cobs rubbed together. Remove cob fragments — cause storage heating.

question: How do I prevent moisture reabsorption after drying?
answer: Store in sealed hermetic bags immediately after reaching target moisture. Do not leave grain in open-mouth sacks — grain reabsorbs moisture from humid air, especially overnight.

question: What is fumigation?
answer: Treating stored grain with chemical gas (Phosphine/Aluminium Phosphide) to kill all insects at all life stages. Requires sealed store and trained operator. Not needed with hermetic bags.

question: Should I save seed for next season?
answer: Open-pollinated varieties (ZM521, Chivaura): YES — save best cobs from healthy plants. Hybrid varieties (SC403, SC627): NO — hybrids do not breed true. Buy new hybrid seed every season.

question: How do I save maize seed?
answer: Select best plants — tall, well-filled cobs, disease-free. Shell central part of cob. Dry to below 12%. Store in sealed container with silica gel. Label with variety and season.

question: How do I save sugar bean seed?
answer: Select healthiest pods from disease-free plants. Dry on plant. Harvest when pods rattle. Dry further to 12%. Store in airtight container with 2-3 dried chillies to deter bean weevil.

question: What is the quality standard for grain sale?
answer: GMB and private buyers require: moisture below 12.5%, free from visible mould, no excess foreign matter, correct weight per bag (90kg standard). Rejected grain loses all value.

question: What is correct bag weight?
answer: Standard: 50kg or 90kg bags depending on buyer. Weigh on calibrated scale. Short-weight bags at GMB are rejected. Overweight bags are not paid for the extra.

question: How do I mill maize at home?
answer: Small plate mills available at $150-300. Sell milling services to neighbours to recover cost. Mealie meal sells at $40-60 per 50kg vs $25-30 for grain — double the margin.

question: What is the price of sugar beans in Zimbabwe?
answer: Sugar bean prices vary seasonally: typically $0.50-0.80/kg at farm gate. Prices highest in March-May (off-season). For your {farm_size} ha at $0.65/kg: significant income potential.

question: What is proper grain sampling for quality testing?
answer: Take samples from multiple depths and positions in storage — top, middle, bottom, corners. Mix for representative sample. Aflatoxin test requires 2kg from at least 10 positions.

question: What is the difference between threshing and shelling?
answer: Threshing: removing grain from seed heads (sorghum, wheat, beans, groundnuts). Shelling: removing maize kernels from cob. Both require dry grain — wet processing damages grain.

question: What is a warehouse receipt system?
answer: Depositing grain in certified warehouse, receiving a receipt usable as collateral for loans. Allows holding grain for better prices without personal storage costs.

question: What is the price of maize in Zimbabwe?
answer: Maize market prices vary. GMB sets a floor price each season. Check current prices at GMB depot or agro-dealer before harvest. For planning: approximately $0.28/kg at farm gate.

question: How do I preserve vegetables after harvest?
answer: Cool quickly after harvest. Store in shade. For short term: cool room or pit storage. For longer: sundrying, pickling, or processing. Leafy vegetables keep 1-2 days at ambient temperature.

question: What is sun drying of vegetables?
answer: Slice thinly, spread on clean rack or cloth, dry in direct sun for 2-5 days. Protected from rain and dust. Dried vegetables keep 6-12 months. Tomatoes, okra, and pumpkin leaves dry well.

question: What is the shelf life of groundnuts?
answer: Properly dried groundnuts (9% moisture) in hermetic bags: 12+ months. Shelled groundnuts are more susceptible than unshelled. Aflatoxin risk increases with storage time — test before export or sale.

question: How do I transport grain safely?
answer: Use clean, dry bags. Weigh before transport. Cover load to protect from rain. Secure bags to prevent movement. Damaged bags allow moisture entry and pest access.

question: What is the economic cost of poor storage?
answer: 15-30% post-harvest losses = {storage_loss_kg} kg lost on your {farm_size} ha yield = ${storage_loss_value} lost income per season. Hermetic bags cost ${bag_cost} and prevent all of this.

question: What is grain bank?
answer: Community-managed grain storage facility where members store grain and can borrow against stored grain during lean periods. Common in Zimbabwe communal areas — ask your ward AGRITEX.

question: How much will I earn this season?
answer: For your {farm_size} ha at {budget} input in Region {region}: expected yield {expected_yield} kg at ${market_price}/kg = ${gross_revenue} gross. After costs: approximately ${net_profit} net profit.

question: What are my expected costs?
answer: For {farm_size} ha at {budget} input: Seed, Fertiliser, Labour, Chemicals, Contingency. Check Planning tab for full breakdown specific to your {crop}.

question: What is ROI in farming?
answer: Return on Investment = (Net profit / Total cost) x 100. Your estimated ROI for {crop} at {budget} input is in the Planning tab. Compare to bank savings rate to assess farming value.

question: What is my break-even yield?
answer: Break-even yield = Total costs / Market price per kg. For your {farm_size} ha: see Planning tab for exact figure. Your expected yield should comfortably exceed break-even.

question: Should I grow maize or sugar beans?
answer: For your {farm_size} ha at {budget} budget: maize is staple food security, sugar beans give higher profit margin ($0.65/kg vs $0.28/kg). Consider intercropping both for best outcome.

question: How do I reduce my farming costs?
answer: Top cost reducers: 1) Save OPV seed. 2) Make compost. 3) Group buy inputs with neighbours (10-15% discount). 4) Use conservation agriculture. 5) Share equipment.

question: How do I access farming finance?
answer: Options in Zimbabwe: ZETREF loans through banks, CBZ agricultural loans, grain marketing input schemes, NGO schemes, VSL (Village Savings and Loan) groups. Start with self-finance.

question: What is a VSL group?
answer: Village Savings and Loan group — members pool savings weekly and lend to each other at low interest. Very effective for smallholder finance. Groups of 15-30 members.

question: Should I hire labour or do it myself?
answer: Labour cost for {farm_size} ha depends on operations needed. At {budget} input, labour is a significant cost. Prioritise your own labour for critical operations: planting, topdress, pest control.

question: What is contract farming and should I do it?
answer: Company provides inputs on credit, you repay at harvest from guaranteed price. Reduces financial risk but restricts crop sale options. Research the company track record before signing.

question: What is crop insurance?
answer: Insurance paying out if yield falls below guaranteed level due to drought or flood. Available through Agribank. Premium about 5% of expected revenue. Consider for large investments.

question: How do I plan a farming budget?
answer: Step 1: List all input costs. Step 2: Estimate yield. Step 3: Estimate revenue. Step 4: Calculate profit. Step 5: Identify cost reductions. Check Planning tab for automated calculation.

question: What is a farming enterprise?
answer: A farming business that generates income. Treat your {farm_size} ha as a business — keep records, calculate profit per crop, compare enterprises, invest in the most profitable.

question: How do I keep farm records?
answer: Record in a notebook: planting date, inputs and costs, weather, scouting findings, yield at harvest, sales price. Review to identify what worked. Update MDUMENI profile each season.

question: What is the profitability of vegetables vs maize?
answer: Vegetables (tomatoes, cabbages) yield $1,000-3,000/ha but require irrigation and skill. Maize is lower return but lower risk. With irrigation: vegetables often more profitable.

question: What is diversification in farming?
answer: Growing multiple crops to spread risk. If maize fails, sugar beans may succeed. For {farm_size} ha: grow maize + sugar beans + small vegetable garden as minimum.

question: What is a farming cooperative?
answer: Farmers pooling resources — buying inputs together for lower prices, selling together for better prices, sharing equipment. Join or start a cooperative at your local agro-dealer or AGRITEX.

question: How do I negotiate a better price for my crop?
answer: Know the market price before you sell. Sell at harvest peak if you have storage. Group sell with other farmers. Offer dry, clean, properly weighed grain — commands premium.

question: What crops give the best profit in Zimbabwe?
answer: Highest profit/ha typically: tobacco (high risk), vegetables with irrigation, groundnuts, sugar beans. For {budget} budget without irrigation in Region {region}: sugar beans and groundnuts lead.

question: How do I plan for input shortages?
answer: Buy inputs before planting season — shortages occur in October-November. Buy lime in August-September. Buy seed in September. Join a cooperative for advance ordering.

question: What is the value of crop rotation on my farm?
answer: Maize after legume saves fertiliser nitrogen. Sugar beans fix 50-150 kg N/ha. Over {farm_size} ha: significant annual saving on AN fertiliser from correct rotation.

question: How do I calculate profit per hectare?
answer: Revenue per ha = yield (kg) x price ($/kg). Costs per ha = all inputs + labour + land prep. Profit per ha = Revenue minus Costs. Check Planning tab for your {crop} calculation.

question: How do I access AGRITEX extension services?
answer: Visit your local AGRITEX office or ward Agricultural Extension Worker (AEW). Services are free. Training, demonstration plots, and input scheme information available.

question: What government farming support is available?
answer: Presidential Input Scheme (subsidised inputs), ZETREF soft loans, AGRITEX free extension, GMB guaranteed purchase, Presidential Mechanisation Programme. Access through district agricultural offices.

question: How do I calculate the cost of my labour?
answer: Track days worked per activity. Standard wage: $3-5/day casual labour. For your {farm_size} ha: land prep, planting, weeding, and harvesting days — total in Planning tab.

question: What is minimum tillage and does it save money?
answer: Minimum tillage saves tractor hire costs and less fuel per hectare. Over {farm_size} ha: meaningful seasonal saving. Also improves soil health and moisture retention long-term.

question: What is the cost of hermetic bag storage vs losses?
answer: Hermetic bags: $2-4 per 50kg bag. Without hermetic: lose 15-30% of grain to weevils. Cost of bags vs loss prevention — bags pay for themselves many times over.

question: How do I price my produce?
answer: Base price on: GMB floor price, local market price, transport cost. Never sell below your break-even price per kg. Know your costs before accepting any offer.

question: What is forward selling?
answer: Agreeing sale price before harvest — reduces price risk but misses upside if prices rise. Useful for cash flow planning. Keep some for higher spot prices.

question: How do I manage cash flow in farming?
answer: Farming has seasonal cash flow: high cost at planting, zero income during growing, income at harvest. Save during good seasons. VSL groups help manage cash between harvests.

question: What is farm gate price vs market price?
answer: Farm gate price: what buyer pays at your farm — lower. Market price: what consumer pays in town — higher. Transporting yourself to market captures more value.

question: Should I invest in a water pump?
answer: A petrol pump ($200-400) enables dry-season vegetable production. Revenue potential: $1,000-2,000 per dry season on 0.2 ha. Payback: 1 season. Best investment with a water source.

question: What is the cost of certified vs saved seed?
answer: Certified hybrid seed: $8-12/kg. Saved OPV seed: $0 (your own). Hybrid yields 20-40% more but costs $40-80/ha more. At {budget} budget: OPV saves significant input cost.

question: What is enterprise budgeting?
answer: Detailed financial plan for one crop on your farm. Lists all costs, expected yield, revenue, and profit. AGRITEX has standard enterprise budgets for Zimbabwe crops.

question: How do I use the MDUMENI planning tool?
answer: The Planning tab shows your complete financial plan for {crop} on {farm_size} ha at {budget} input: costs breakdown, expected yield, revenue, and ROI. Switch scenarios to compare.

question: What is the payback period for irrigation equipment?
answer: Basic drip system for 0.2 ha: $200-400. Revenue increase from dry-season vegetables: $500-1,500 per season. Payback: 1-2 seasons. Borehole: $3,000-5,000 — longer payback.

question: What are the main input costs in Zimbabwe?
answer: Compound D 50kg: $15-22. AN 34.5% 50kg: $20-28. Maize seed (certified) 10kg: $8-12. Sugar bean seed 1kg: $1.50-2.50. Herbicide per ha: $8-15. Insecticide per ha: $10-25.

question: How do I reduce fertiliser costs?
answer: 1) Correct pH first — fertiliser is wasted in acidic soil. 2) Make compost. 3) Use legume rotation for nitrogen. 4) Group buy in bulk. 5) Apply at correct timing for maximum uptake.

question: What is the cost of tractor hire in Zimbabwe?
answer: Tractor hire for ploughing and discing: $40-80 per hour. For {farm_size} ha: approximately 3-5 hours needed. Conservation agriculture (ripping only): 1-2 hours. Oxen: $15-25 per day.

question: What is the break-even price for my produce?
answer: Break-even price = Total cost per ha / Expected yield per ha. If your costs are $300/ha and expected yield is 2,500 kg: break-even = $0.12/kg. Current maize price (~$0.28/kg) gives good margin.

question: How do I access a bank loan for farming?
answer: Requirements typically: farm plan, proof of land, ID, collateral. Banks: Agribank (agriculture specialist), CBZ, FBC. Cooperatives have better loan access than individuals. ZETREF is specifically for farmers.

question: What is seasonal price variation for maize?
answer: Maize prices: lowest at harvest (March-April), rise through May-August, peak at planting season shortage (October-November). Store with hermetic bags and sell in June-August for 20-40% premium.

question: How much does farming insurance cost in Zimbabwe?
answer: Weather index insurance for maize: approximately 5-8% of expected gross revenue. For {farm_size} ha: roughly $25-60/season. Pays out if rainfall falls below index threshold.

question: What is the profitability of groundnuts?
answer: Groundnuts: 1.5-3 t/ha at medium input. Farm gate price: $0.60-1.00/kg unshelled. For {farm_size} ha: $900-3,000 gross. Higher labour cost but excellent rotation crop after maize.

question: What is the profitability of sesame?
answer: Sesame: 0.4-1.2 t/ha, price $1.20-2.50/kg — highest value crop for Region IV-V. Low input requirements. For {farm_size} ha in suitable region: $480-3,000 gross from very low inputs.

question: What are cash crops vs food crops?
answer: Food crops: primarily for household consumption (maize, cowpeas, sweet potato). Cash crops: primarily for sale (tobacco, cotton, sesame, vegetables). Mix both for food security and income.

question: How do I plan my land allocation?
answer: For {farm_size} ha: allocate 70% to main food crop (maize), 20% to cash or legume crop (sugar beans/groundnuts), 10% to dry-season vegetables (with irrigation). Adjust based on market access.

question: What farming activities should I do this month?
answer: In {month} for {crop}: check the Calendar tab for today's specific tasks with detailed instructions for your crop stage.

question: When should I start land preparation?
answer: In Region {region}: start land preparation in September-October. Deep plough (25cm) first time, then disc to break clods. Complete at least 2 weeks before planting.

question: What is the best planting month for my region?
answer: Region {region} optimal planting window: October-December. Plant at first reliable rains in moist soil. Do not plant dry and wait for rain.

question: When do first rains usually arrive?
answer: In Region {region}: first rains expected October-November. Wait for confirmation of seasonal rains — 25mm+ over 3-5 days. Watch forecast before planting.

question: What crops can I grow in the dry season?
answer: Dry season crops requiring irrigation: cabbages, tomatoes, onions, garlic, rape, spinach, butternuts. Your irrigation status: {irrigation_status}.

question: What happens in the vegetative stage?

question: What happens at the reproductive stage?
answer: Flowering, pollination, and grain fill. Most critical for yield. Drought or pest damage here causes permanent yield loss. Ensure adequate moisture and scout daily.

question: What is the growing season length in Zimbabwe?
answer: Season length by region: Region I: 180+ frost-free days. Region II: 160-180 days. Region III: 140-160 days. Region IV: 120-140 days. Region V: under 120 days.

question: When is harvest time for maize?
answer: In Region {region}: maize planted in October-November harvests in March-April. ZM521 (120 days): approximately March. SC403 (90 days): approximately January-February.

question: What should I do after harvest?
answer: Post-harvest tasks: 1) Shell and dry grain. 2) Store in hermetic bags. 3) Clear crop residues. 4) Test soil pH. 5) Plan next crop rotation. 6) Check stored grain weekly.

question: What do I do with crop residues?
answer: Options: 1) Incorporate for organic matter. 2) Mulch for conservation agriculture. 3) Compost. 4) Feed to livestock. 5) Burn only as last resort — destroys organic matter.

question: When should I apply lime?
answer: Apply lime ideally 4-8 weeks before planting. At your current pH {ph}: {lime_urgency}. In Region {region}: apply August-September for November planting.

question: When should I apply Compound D?

question: When should I apply AN topdress?

question: What is the inter-seasonal period?
answer: Period between harvest and next planting — typically May-October in Region {region}. Use for: soil tests, lime application, land prep, sourcing inputs, farm planning.

question: When do I scout for Fall Armyworm?
answer: Scout weekly from emergence to V8 stage. Scout in early morning. Check 20 plants per hectare. At high risk periods (October-December): scout twice weekly.

question: What is the critical weed-free period?
answer: Keep crop weed-free for first 6 weeks (V1-V6). Weeds after 6 weeks cause minimal yield loss. First weeding at V2-V3 (14-21 days). Second weeding at V6 (35-40 days) with topdress.

question: What is the risk of frost?
answer: Frost risk in Zimbabwe: mainly May-August in highveld above 1,500m. Region I and parts of Region II. Plan to harvest before May in frost-prone areas.

question: What is the risk of dry spells in my region?
answer: Region {region} dry spell risk: most dangerous during mid-season January-February at tasselling/silking. Monitor forecasts. Irrigate if available.

question: When should I plant a second crop?
answer: After early-maturing first crop: opportunity for second fast crop (sugar beans 90 days, cowpeas 70 days) if rains permit. Region {region} second crop potential depends on rainfall.

question: What is ENSO and how does it affect my farming?
answer: El Nino-Southern Oscillation causes dry or wet seasons in Zimbabwe. El Nino: dry — plant drought-tolerant varieties. La Nina: wet — improve drainage, fast-maturing varieties. Check ENSO forecast each season.

question: When is the best time to buy inputs?
answer: Buy inputs in August-September before seasonal demand spike. Prices rise 15-25% by October-November. Seed, lime, and Compound D can be bought and stored safely.

question: What is the critical growth period for sugar beans?
answer: Sugar beans are most sensitive at: germination (days 1-7), flowering (days 35-45), and pod fill (days 50-70). Ensure adequate moisture at these stages.

question: When should I harvest groundnuts?
answer: Groundnuts mature 110-130 days after planting. Harvest indicator: dig sample plants — shells should show dark veining inside. Yellow leaves on most plants indicates maturity.

question: What is the optimal temperature for maize germination?
answer: Maize germinates best at 21-35C soil temperature. Below 10C — very slow or no germination. Your soil at {temp}C is suitable for germination.

question: What is the impact of late planting?
answer: Each week of late planting beyond optimal window reduces maize yield by 5-8% in Region {region}. Planting 3 weeks late: potential 15-24% yield reduction. Prioritise timely planting.

question: What are the signs that harvest is approaching?
answer: Signs of approaching maturity: leaves yellowing, husks turning papery, silk completely dry, grain firm and dented, black layer forming. Your crop at day {days_planted}: check Calendar tab.

question: What is the off-season crop calendar?
answer: May-June: soil testing, lime, land prep. July-August: compost, input purchase, equipment maintenance. September: dry-season vegetable planting (with irrigation). October: main season start.

question: When is the best time to apply manure?
answer: Apply manure 4-6 weeks before planting to allow incorporation and breakdown. Rate: 5-10 t/ha. Farmyard manure adds N, P, K, and organic matter.

question: How do I track my crop progress?
answer: Use the MDUMENI Calendar tab — shows your current phase, days elapsed, days to harvest, and today's tasks. Update your planting date in Settings if needed.

question: What are the consequences of skipping topdress?
answer: Skipping AN topdress at V6 typically reduces maize yield by 20-40%. For your {farm_size} ha: significant potential yield loss. The topdress investment has very high return.

question: What is the recommended herbicide timing?
answer: Pre-emergence herbicide (Atrazine): apply within 72 hours of planting. Post-emergence (Nicosulfuron): apply at V3-V5. Do not apply in hot conditions or when crop is stressed.

question: How many seasons per year can I farm?
answer: Main season: November-April (rain-fed). Dry season: May-October (irrigation required). Without irrigation: 1 season/year. With irrigation: up to 2 seasons for fast-maturing crops.

question: When should I apply a fungicide?
answer: Preventive: spray at first sign of disease or when conditions favour disease (humid, warm). Curative: apply within 48 hours of symptom appearance. Follow Calendar tab timing.

question: What is the impact of early rains on farming?
answer: Early rains before optimal planting window tempt early planting — risk dry spell. Wait for confirmation of seasonal rains — 25mm+ over 3-5 days before planting.

question: When should I weed for maximum benefit?
answer: Weed at V2-V3 (14-21 days) — most critical timing. Second weed at V6 (35-40 days). After 6 weeks, weeding has minimal yield benefit. Combine second weeding with topdress application.

question: What is the relationship between planting date and pest pressure?
answer: Early planting (optimal window) reduces Fall Armyworm pressure — crop passes vulnerable stage before peak armyworm populations. Late planting exposes V3-V6 to peak pressure.

question: When do I apply lime for best results?
answer: 4-8 weeks before planting for maximum effect. August-September for Region {region} November planting. Your current pH {ph}: {lime_urgency}.

question: What is the growing degree day concept?
answer: Growing degree days accumulate heat above 10C base temperature. Maize needs 1,200-1,800 growing degree days to mature depending on variety. Useful for predicting harvest timing.

question: How do I plan my farming calendar?
answer: Key dates for Region {region}: August-September: lime and land prep. October: input buying, first rains watch. November: plant at first reliable rains. December-February: main management. March-April: harvest.

question: What is the cotton farming calendar?
answer: Cotton (Region II-III): plant October-November with first rains. Harvest April-June. Requires rigorous pest management (bollworm). Sells through Cottco and private buyers.

question: When should I rotate crops?
answer: Rotate every season — never plant the same crop family in the same field two seasons in a row. Maize this season: legume next season. Rotation is most important agronomic practice.

question: What is a seasonal forecast and how do I use it?
answer: Seasonal forecast from MeteoZim predicts above/below normal rainfall for the coming season. If dry season forecast: choose drought-tolerant varieties. Wet forecast: normal planting, improve drainage.

question: What are the early warning signs of crop failure?
answer: Poor germination after 10-14 days. Widespread yellowing at V2-V3. More than 30% pest infestation. Wilting despite adequate moisture. Identify early — options decrease as season progresses.

question: How do I plan if the rains are late?
answer: Late rains (after December): switch to faster-maturing variety (ZM309: 90 days, SC403: 90 days). Reduce plant population. Focus on drought-tolerant crops (sorghum, cowpeas, groundnuts).

question: What is the risk of hail damage?
answer: Hail risk: highest during November-February in Zimbabwe. Hail causes physical damage to leaves and young ears. Insurance helps. Replant immediately if hail occurs before V6.

question: What is the difference between hybrid and OPV seed?
answer: Hybrid seed: crosses of two pure lines — high yield, uniform, but cannot be saved. OPV (Open Pollinated Variety): lower yield but seed can be saved. At {budget} budget: {seed_type_rec}.

question: What is ZM521?
answer: ZM521 is an Open Pollinated Variety maize developed by CIMMYT for Zimbabwe. Maturity 120 days. Yield 2.5-4.5 t/ha. Moderate drought tolerance. Streak-tolerant. Seed can be saved.

question: What is SC403?
answer: SC403 (Seed Co) is a hybrid maize — 90-day maturity, very high yield (6-8 t/ha) but requires medium-high inputs. Good drought tolerance. Do not save seed.

question: What is SC627?
answer: SC627 (Seed Co) is a high-yielding hybrid — 120 days, 9-12 t/ha at high input. Requires irrigation or reliable 700mm+ rainfall. High fertiliser response. Regions I-II only.

question: What seed is best for drought conditions?
answer: Most drought-tolerant varieties: ZM309 (90 days, drought tolerant OPV), Pannar PAN53 (drought-bred hybrid), SC403 (drought-tolerant hybrid). At {budget} budget: ZM309 is cost-effective.

question: What is ZM309?
answer: ZM309 is a short-season (90-day) OPV developed for drought-prone areas. Yield 2-3.5 t/ha. Saves well as OPV. Best for Regions III-IV or as risk management in dry years.

question: What maize variety is best for Region II?
answer: Region II at {budget} budget: ZM521 (OPV, low budget), SC403 (hybrid, medium budget), SC627 (hybrid, high budget with irrigation). Your profile suggests: {seed_rec}.

question: What is the difference between yellow and white maize?
answer: White maize: preferred for human consumption (sadza) in Zimbabwe — commands premium price at GMB. Yellow maize: preferred for animal feed. Grow white maize for food and market sale.

question: What sugar bean varieties grow in Zimbabwe?
answer: Common Zimbabwe sugar bean varieties: Chivaura, Carioca, Lyamungu 85, PAN 9216. Chivaura: OPV, can save seed, 90 days, good drought tolerance.

question: What groundnut varieties grow in Zimbabwe?
answer: Main varieties: Falcon (medium, high yield), Uyashe (large-seeded for export). Confectionery groundnuts (Falcon, Uyashe) command higher prices than oil groundnuts.

question: What sorghum varieties grow in Zimbabwe?
answer: Improved varieties: SV2 (white, 110 days), Macia (white, 95 days), Kuyuma (red, drought tolerant). White sorghum preferred for human consumption.

question: What is pearl millet (mhunga)?
answer: Pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum) — very drought tolerant, grows in Region IV-V where maize fails. Varieties: Okashana, Trossard. 90-100 days. High iron and zinc content.

question: What is sesame (mutsvudzwa)?
answer: Sesame (Sesamum indicum) — drought-tolerant cash crop for Region IV-V. Short-season (90 days). Requires well-drained soil. High market value $1.20-2.50/kg. Growing export market.

question: What is cowpea (nyemba)?
answer: Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) — fast-growing legume (70-80 days), drought tolerant, fixes nitrogen. Dual purpose — grain and leaves as vegetable. Very important in Region IV-V.

question: What is the shelf life of purchased seed?
answer: Properly stored seed: maize hybrid 1 year, OPV 2 years, sugar beans 2 years, groundnuts 1 year. Store in cool, dry, sealed container. Above 25C rapidly reduces germination.

question: How do I test seed germination before planting?
answer: Place 10 seeds between wet cloth. Keep at room temperature. Check after 5-7 days. Germination rate: 90%+ excellent, 80-90% acceptable, below 70% — increase seed rate or buy new seed.

question: What is hybrid vigour?
answer: Hybrid vigour (heterosis) is the improved performance of F1 hybrids over their parents — bigger, more uniform, higher yielding. Lost in F2 generation — reason not to save hybrid seed.

question: How do I spot counterfeit seed?
answer: Check: official Seed Authority label and batch number. Seed is uniform in size and colour. Germination test result on label. Suspicious price (too cheap). Buy from reputable agro-dealers only.

question: What is seed certification?
answer: Government verification that seed meets purity, germination, and moisture standards. Look for: Seed Control Authority of Zimbabwe (SCAZ) certification tag on bag. Never buy uncertified seed.

question: What vegetable varieties do well in Zimbabwe?
answer: Tomatoes: Rodade (determinate, heat-tolerant). Cabbages: Conquistador. Onions: Texas Grano. Butternuts: Butterscotch. All require good soil, correct pH, and irrigation.

question: What is a variety trial?
answer: Comparing multiple varieties side-by-side under same conditions to identify best performer for local conditions. AGRITEX and seed companies run national trials. Ask your extension officer.

question: How do I store saved seed safely?
answer: Shell/thresh, dry to 12% moisture, clean thoroughly, store in airtight container (tin, bottle, sealed bag), add silica gel sachet or dried chilli peppers. Label: variety, date, source.

question: What is seed selection in open-pollinated varieties?
answer: Select seed from: highest-yielding, most uniform, healthiest plants. Avoid: odd plants, disease-affected, earliest or latest to mature. Maintain genetic diversity by selecting from multiple plants.

question: What is the seed rate for sugar beans?
